bow-wow-wow.aboutKids: A friendly dog says bow wow, and someone asks who he belongs to. He is little Tom Tinker's dog!
bow-wow-wow.story: This tiny dog rhyme is anonymous. It was printed around 1765 in Mother Goose's Melody, one of the first English nursery-rhyme books, under the title Caesar's Song. Later collections, including 19th-century American picture books, kept it alive, sometimes renaming the owner Tom Tucker. Little Duet sets the words to its own simple chant.
bow-wow-wow.funFact: In one of the very first nursery-rhyme books, printed around 1765, this little dog rhyme appeared under the title Caesar's Song.

jack-be-nimble.aboutKids: Quick, quick! Jack is a speedy, bouncy boy who jumps right over a candlestick in one big leap.
jack-be-nimble.story: An anonymous English rhyme, first found handwritten in a manuscript of about 1815 and printed by James Orchard Halliwell in 1844. It may echo an old custom of jumping over candlesticks, both as a sport and as a way of telling fortunes. It is usually chanted rather than sung.
jack-be-nimble.funFact: Children have long used it as a jump-rope rhyme, which is why it is more often chanted than sung.

rain-rain-go-away.aboutKids: It is raining, and a little one wants to go outside and play, so they kindly ask the rain to go away.
rain-rain-go-away.story: Children have chanted rain charms for centuries. James Howell's 1659 proverb collection has an early version sending the rain to Spain, and John Aubrey (1687) noted children asking it to return another day. The familiar wording, with a child who wants to play, appears in Halliwell's 1844 collection. It is sung to the playground sol-mi-la chant.
rain-rain-go-away.funFact: Older versions told the rain to go away to Spain, or asked it to come back again on Saturday instead.
rain-rain-go-away.myth: Sometimes said to be about the Spanish Armada of 1588. No evidence links it to the Armada; the earliest record (1659) is simply a weather charm, and similar rain rhymes exist in many cultures.

see-saw-margery-daw.aboutKids: Up and down, up and down! Margery goes for a ride on a seesaw, rocking high and then low.
see-saw-margery-daw.story: An anonymous rhyme first printed around 1765 in Mother Goose's Melody, a London collection. It may have begun as a work chant for pairs of sawyers pulling a long saw back and forth, and later became a seesaw game. No real Margery Daw is known; the name probably just rhymes.
see-saw-margery-daw.funFact: A London play from 1640 already linked a see-saw chant to workers sawing wood together, more than a century before this rhyme was printed.

star-light-star-bright.aboutKids: When the very first star twinkles in the evening sky, you make a quiet wish and hope it comes true.
star-light-star-bright.story: An anonymous American wishing rhyme, first written down in the 1860s and 1870s, when it was linked to fortune-telling. The custom of wishing on the first star of the evening may be older than the rhyme itself. It reached Britain by the early 20th century and is usually spoken, not sung.
star-light-star-bright.funFact: Families traditionally say it the moment they spot the first star of the evening, and then make a wish.

bingo.writtenBy: Traditional English song; c. 1780 sheet music attributed to William Swords
bingo.aboutKids: A farmer has a happy dog named Bingo, and everyone spells his name together, clapping in place of letters.
bingo.story: The earliest trace is sheet music from about 1780 credited to William Swords, an actor at London's Haymarket Theatre, with the dog then often called little Bingo. It was reprinted in 1785, noted in the United States by 1842, and grew into a spelling and clapping game for children.
bingo.funFact: In some places the dog had other names, like Bango or Pinto, and sometimes his owner was a miller or a shepherd.

hush-little-baby.aboutKids: A grown-up softly sings to a sleepy baby, promising one lovely present after another, like a singing mockingbird and a shiny ring.
hush-little-baby.story: A lullaby from the Southern United States with no known author. The English collector Cecil Sharp wrote down a version in Franklin County, Virginia, in 1918, the earliest on record. Its chain of promised gifts follows an old swapping-song pattern. Folk singers such as Jean Ritchie, Burl Ives and Joan Baez spread it widely.
hush-little-baby.funFact: The earliest written version dates from 1918, when a visiting English song collector heard it sung in Virginia.

jack-and-jill.writtenBy: Traditional English nursery rhyme. Tune: James William Elliott
jack-and-jill.aboutKids: Jack and Jill climb up a hill to fetch a pail of water, then take a big tumble all the way down.
jack-and-jill.story: An anonymous rhyme first printed around 1765 in Mother Goose's Melody, where the girl's name was spelled Gill. Jack and Jill was already an everyday English phrase for any boy and girl. The tune most families sing was published by James William Elliott in National Nursery Rhymes and Nursery Songs (1870).
jack-and-jill.funFact: In the earliest printed version, more than 250 years ago, Jill's name was spelled Gill.
jack-and-jill.myth: Claimed to hide stories about a Norse moon legend, a tax on drink measures under Charles I, Tudor politicians, or a couple from a Somerset village. These ideas mostly appeared after the rhyme was printed and have no supporting evidence.

london-bridge.writtenBy: Traditional English nursery rhyme and singing game
london-bridge.aboutKids: Two children make a bridge with their arms, everyone sings that it is falling down, and the bridge gently catches a friend.
london-bridge.story: A singing game of unknown authorship. Dancing the building of London Bridge is mentioned in a play written around 1636, and the words were printed in Tommy Thumb's Pretty Song Book around 1744. The tune families know today was first printed in 1879, in A. H. Rosewig's American collection of songs and games.
london-bridge.funFact: A real London Bridge, built in 1831, was taken apart stone by stone and rebuilt in Lake Havasu City, Arizona.
london-bridge.myth: Often said to recall a Viking attack on the bridge in 1014, or a legend of a person sealed into its foundations. The Viking 'evidence' is an 1844 translation shaped by the rhyme itself, and neither theory is proven.

old-macdonald.aboutKids: Old MacDonald has a busy farm full of animals, and each one makes its own noisy sound, from moo to oink to quack.
old-macdonald.story: A folk song of unknown authorship. A similar farmyard song appears in Thomas d'Urfey's opera of 1706, and English collectors found versions in the 1900s. An early printing called Ohio, with a farmer named Old Macdougal, appeared in Tommy's Tunes (1917), a book of First World War songs. Recordings in the 1920s settled the familiar name and tune.
old-macdonald.funFact: The farmer was not always MacDonald. A 1917 version called him Old Macdougal, and his famous name only settled in during the 1920s.

pat-a-cake.aboutKids: Clap, clap! We help the baker make a cake, pat it, mark it with a letter, and pop it in the oven.
pat-a-cake.story: This clapping rhyme first appears in Thomas D'Urfey's play The Campaigners (1698), recited by a nurse to the children in her care, and it was probably older still. A different wording was printed in Mother Goose's Melody around 1765, and James Hook set it to music in 1796. Little Duet uses its own sol-mi-la chant.
pat-a-cake.funFact: Grown-ups have played this clapping game with little ones for over 300 years, often swapping in the child's own initial.

ring-around-the-rosie.year: 1881 (words first printed in English); melody reported c. 1790
ring-around-the-rosie.origin: England and the United States, with European relatives
ring-around-the-rosie.aboutKids: Friends hold hands, skip around in a circle, and then everyone falls down together with a giggle.
ring-around-the-rosie.story: An anonymous ring game. A related rhyme was printed in Germany in 1796 and versions were noted in the US in the 1840s. The familiar English words appeared in Kate Greenaway's Mother Goose (1881) and William Wells Newell's Games and Songs of American Children (1883). Many early versions had no falling down at all.
ring-around-the-rosie.funFact: In many old versions, players ended with a curtsy or a bow instead of tumbling to the ground.
ring-around-the-rosie.myth: Widely said to describe the Great Plague of 1665 or the Black Death. Folklorists reject this: the plague reading only appeared in the mid-20th century, and the earliest versions lack the sneezing and falling it relies on.

alphabet-song.writtenBy: Words: unknown, published by Charles Bradlee. Tune: French melody 'Ah! vous dirai-je, maman'
alphabet-song.aboutKids: We sing every letter from A all the way to Z, so we can learn our ABCs together.
alphabet-song.story: The Boston music publisher Charles Bradlee copyrighted the song in 1835 as The A.B.C., a German air with variations for the flute. Who wrote the words is unknown. The melody is the French tune also used for Twinkle Twinkle Little Star, first printed in 1761.
alphabet-song.funFact: The same tune helps children learn their alphabets in many languages, including Spanish, German, French, Japanese and Korean.
alphabet-song.myth: Often said that Mozart composed the tune. He wrote twelve piano variations on it around 1781-82, but the melody had already been printed in France in 1761.

twinkle-twinkle.writtenBy: Words: Jane Taylor. Tune: French melody 'Ah! vous dirai-je, maman' (composer unknown)
twinkle-twinkle.aboutKids: A child looks up at a tiny, sparkly star in the night sky and wonders what it is.
twinkle-twinkle.story: Jane Taylor wrote the poem The Star, published in 1806 in Rhymes for the Nursery, a book she wrote with her sister Ann. The words were later joined to a French tune first printed in 1761, and appeared together in print by 1838. Only the first of its five verses is widely sung today.
twinkle-twinkle.funFact: In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, the Mad Hatter sings a silly version about a twinkling little bat.
twinkle-twinkle.myth: Mozart did not write the tune. He composed twelve piano variations on the existing French melody in Vienna around 1781-82.

baa-baa-black-sheep.writtenBy: Traditional English nursery rhyme. Tune: French melody 'Ah! vous dirai-je, maman'
baa-baa-black-sheep.aboutKids: A woolly black sheep kindly shares three bags of wool, enough for everyone, even a little boy down the lane.
baa-baa-black-sheep.story: An anonymous rhyme printed around 1744 in Tommy Thumb's Pretty Song Book, with words very close to today's. It is sung to a version of the French tune also used for Twinkle Twinkle Little Star; words and melody were first printed together in 1879.
baa-baa-black-sheep.funFact: In 1951 an early computer in Manchester, England, played it, making it one of the first tunes ever played by a computer.
baa-baa-black-sheep.myth: Often said to protest a medieval wool tax (1275) or to carry a hidden meaning about slavery. The slavery claim has no historical basis, and the tax idea is speculation about a rhyme first printed centuries later.

mulberry-bush.aboutKids: Friends dance around a bush, then act out their busy day: washing hands, brushing hair, and getting ready.
mulberry-bush.story: An anonymous circle game. Robert Chambers noted a version in Scotland in 1842, and James Orchard Halliwell recorded it in England in 1849, comparing it to a similar bramble-bush game. Players circle, then mime everyday chores. Its tune is the one Nancy Dawson danced to in The Beggar's Opera in 18th-century London.
mulberry-bush.funFact: Mulberries actually grow on trees, not bushes, and an older version of the game may have gone around a bramble bush.
mulberry-bush.myth: Said to have started with women prisoners walking round a mulberry tree at Wakefield Prison. The story comes from one local historian and is unproven.

hey-diddle-diddle.aboutKids: A silly, giggly night: a cat plays the fiddle, a cow jumps over the moon, and a dish runs off with a spoon.
hey-diddle-diddle.story: An anonymous nonsense rhyme first printed around 1765 in Mother Goose's Melody, though the cat-and-fiddle image is far older; a London inn bore that name by 1587. The Opies called it probably the best-known nonsense verse in English. The usual tune was published by James William Elliott in 1870.
hey-diddle-diddle.funFact: When people say they are over the moon because they are very happy, they are borrowing a phrase from this rhyme.
hey-diddle-diddle.myth: Many hidden meanings have been proposed, from historical figures to constellations or the Egyptian goddess Hathor. None is supported; most scholars treat it as pure nonsense verse.

humpty-dumpty.writtenBy: Traditional English nursery rhyme (originally a riddle). Tune: James William Elliott
humpty-dumpty.aboutKids: Humpty Dumpty sits up high on a wall, wobbles, and tumbles down. Even the king's helpers cannot put him back together.
humpty-dumpty.story: This anonymous rhyme was first printed in Samuel Arnold's Juvenile Amusements (1797), with wording different from today's. It probably began as a riddle whose answer was an egg, though the rhyme never says so. Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass (1871) made Humpty a famous egg character; the usual tune comes from James William Elliott (1870).
humpty-dumpty.funFact: The rhyme never actually says Humpty is an egg. It started as a riddle, and an egg was the answer.
humpty-dumpty.myth: Popularly said to be a cannon on a church wall at the 1648 siege of Colchester, or King Richard III. The cannon story traces to a 1996 tourist website and invented verses; neither theory has evidence.

row-row-row-your-boat.writtenBy: Traditional American song; familiar tune credited to Eliphalet Oram Lyte
row-row-row-your-boat.aboutKids: We row our little boat gently down a quiet stream, smiling and happy, as if life were a lovely dream.
row-row-row-your-boat.story: An American song whose words were first printed in 1852 with a different tune. The melody sung today first appeared in The Franklin Square Song Collection (New York, 1881), credited to Eliphalet Oram Lyte, though it is unclear whether he composed or arranged it. It is usually sung as a round.
row-row-row-your-boat.funFact: It is a round: up to four groups start singing one after another, and the overlapping parts make harmony.

farmer-in-the-dell.writtenBy: Traditional singing game, probably of German origin
farmer-in-the-dell.aboutKids: A farmer stands in the middle of a circle and picks friends one by one, all the way to a mouse and some cheese.
farmer-in-the-dell.story: A circle game that probably came from Germany, where a version was recorded in 1826, and was carried to America by immigrants. It was first printed in the US in William Wells Newell's Games and Songs of American Children (1883). Each verse adds a new player to the middle of the ring.
farmer-in-the-dell.funFact: At the end, the last player chosen, the cheese, stands all by themselves in the middle and often becomes the next farmer.

itsy-bitsy-spider.aboutKids: A tiny spider climbs up a water spout. Rain washes it down, the sun comes out to dry everything, and up it climbs again.
itsy-bitsy-spider.story: No one knows who made it up. The earliest known print is a 'Spider Song' in Arthur Walbridge North's travel book Camp and Camino in Lower California (1910), with more grown-up wording. Children's versions with hand motions were printed in 1948, including in Ruth Crawford Seeger's American Folk Songs for Children.
itsy-bitsy-spider.funFact: In Britain and Australia the same little spider has a different name: Incy Wincy Spider.
itsy-bitsy-spider.myth: Online claims that the rhyme secretly has a dark meaning (for example, a warning about tipsy travellers on trains) have no credible source. It is simply a fingerplay about a determined spider.

happy-birthday.writtenBy: Melody: Mildred J. Hill (from 'Good Morning to All', words by Patty Smith Hill). Birthday words: author unknown
happy-birthday.year: 1893 (melody); 1912 (birthday words and melody in print together)
happy-birthday.aboutKids: Everyone sings together to make someone feel special on their birthday, the day they were born.
happy-birthday.story: Kentucky sisters Mildred and Patty Hill, teachers of young children, published the tune as a classroom greeting, 'Good Morning to All', in 1893. Birthday words spread by singing and were printed with the tune by 1912. A long copyright dispute ended when a US court approved a 2016 settlement declaring the song public domain.
happy-birthday.funFact: Guinness World Records has called it the most recognized song in the English language.
happy-birthday.myth: It is often said that Patty Hill wrote the birthday words. That has never been proven; historian Robert Brauneis says no one knows who first sang birthday words to the tune.

brahms-lullaby.writtenBy: Music: Johannes Brahms. German words: Des Knaben Wunderhorn folk collection, second verse adapted from Georg Scherer. English words: traditional
brahms-lullaby.aboutKids: A soft, swaying song that helps a baby close their eyes, snuggle in, and drift off to sleep.
brahms-lullaby.story: Brahms wrote this Wiegenlied (cradle song) in 1868 as a gift for his friend Bertha Faber when her second son was born. The publisher Simrock issued it that November, and it was first performed publicly in Vienna in December 1869, with Clara Schumann at the piano. It soon became one of the most famous lullabies anywhere.
brahms-lullaby.funFact: Brahms hid a little tune in the piano part: a Viennese song Bertha used to sing to him years earlier, when they first met.

jingle-bells.aboutKids: Friends ride a horse-drawn sleigh across the snow, with little bells jingling and everyone laughing as they go.
jingle-bells.story: James Lord Pierpont copyrighted the song in 1857 as 'One Horse Open Sleigh', and it was republished as Jingle Bells in 1859. It is a winter sleigh-ride song and never mentions Christmas; it became a holiday favorite later, helped by Bing Crosby and the Andrews Sisters' 1943 recording.
jingle-bells.funFact: In December 1965, Gemini 6 astronauts played it on a tiny harmonica and bells, the first song played in space.
jingle-bells.myth: A popular story says Pierpont wrote it for a Thanksgiving program at his father's Sunday school. This is unproven, as is Medford, Massachusetts' claim that he wrote it at a local tavern in 1850.

rock-a-bye-baby.writtenBy: Words: Traditional English nursery rhyme. Tune: Effie I. Canning (born Effie Crockett)
rock-a-bye-baby.aboutKids: A grown-up gently rocks a sleepy baby, swaying softly like tree branches in a breeze, until the baby falls asleep.
rock-a-bye-baby.story: The words first appeared in Mother Goose's Melody, printed in London around 1765. The tune most people sing came much later: Effie Crockett said she made it up as a teenager in Massachusetts. Published in 1886 under the name Effie I. Canning after it was used in the play The Old Homestead, it sold strongly as sheet music.
rock-a-bye-baby.funFact: Effie Canning said she was only about 15 when she made up the famous tune.
rock-a-bye-baby.myth: Popular claims that the rhyme was inspired by Native American cradles hung in trees, a woman living in a Derbyshire yew tree, or a political joke about King James II are unproven guesses; the Opies record them without endorsing any.

my-little-ducklings.writtenBy: Traditional German folk song ('Alle meine Entchen'). English words: Little Duet
my-little-ducklings.aboutKids: A family of little ducks paddles across the water, dipping their heads down and lifting their tails up high.
my-little-ducklings.story: Alle meine Entchen is perhaps the best-known children's song in the German-speaking world, and no one knows who wrote it. The tune appears in 18th-century dance manuscripts, one dated around 1750. The words were first printed in Wilhelm Raabe's 1859 novel, where he called it a children's rhyme.
my-little-ducklings.funFact: Its tune climbs up step by step like a staircase, so it is often one of the first songs German children learn on an instrument.

cuckoo-calls.writtenBy: Words: August Heinrich Hoffmann von Fallersleben. Tune: traditional Austrian and Bavarian folk melody. English words: Little Duet
cuckoo-calls.aboutKids: A cuckoo bird calls from the woods to tell everyone that winter is over and spring is here.
cuckoo-calls.story: The poet Hoffmann von Fallersleben wrote this spring poem in 1835 and published it in 1837. In 1842 it was printed with an older folk tune known around Vienna and Bavaria since about 1817. The cuckoo words slowly replaced the old ones and became a staple of kindergartens and family singing.
cuckoo-calls.funFact: Before it was about a cuckoo, the same tune was sung about a little goldfinch who was feeling poorly.

doctor-foster.aboutKids: Doctor Foster walks to the town of Gloucester on a rainy day and splashes right into a very big puddle.
doctor-foster.story: The rhyme was first printed in its familiar form by James Orchard Halliwell in 1844, though a different rhyme about a Dr. Foster going to Gloucester appeared in 1810. Its author is unknown. Gloucester is a real English city, and the short, bouncy verse has been passed between parents and children ever since.
doctor-foster.funFact: The rhyme pairs 'puddle' with 'middle', which may hint at an older word, 'piddle', meaning a small stream.
doctor-foster.myth: A popular theory says the rhyme is about King Edward I getting stuck in mud in Gloucester and refusing to return. It was only a suggestion (Boyd Smith, 1920); there is no evidence, and the Ballad Index finds it unconvincing.

going-home-largo.writtenBy: Music: Antonin Dvorak. English words: Little Duet
going-home-largo.origin: Czech composer, written in the United States
going-home-largo.aboutKids: A slow, gentle tune about the cozy feeling of going home, where the people who love you are waiting.
going-home-largo.story: Dvorak wrote his Symphony 'From the New World' in 1893 while directing a music school in New York. It premiered at Carnegie Hall that December. In the slow Largo movement, a solo English horn plays this calm melody. Dvorak said the movement was linked to Longfellow's poem The Song of Hiawatha.
going-home-largo.funFact: Astronaut Neil Armstrong took a tape recording of the New World Symphony with him on the Apollo 11 Moon landing mission in 1969.
going-home-largo.myth: Many people believe the melody is an old spiritual. It is Dvorak's own tune; the song Goin' Home was created in 1922 when his former student William Arms Fisher set words to it.

little-boy-blue.aboutKids: Little Boy Blue is meant to look after the sheep and cows, but he has curled up for a nap under a haystack.
little-boy-blue.story: The rhyme was printed in London around 1744, in one of the earliest books of nursery rhymes, and is probably older. No author is known. It is most likely just what it seems: a picture of a young farm helper who should be blowing his horn to call the animals but has fallen asleep.
little-boy-blue.funFact: Shakespeare's play King Lear includes lines about a shepherd and sheep in the corn that may echo this very old rhyme.
little-boy-blue.myth: A popular claim says Little Boy Blue was Cardinal Thomas Wolsey. The idea comes from Katherine Elwes Thomas (1930); the Opies and later researchers reject it.

lucy-locket.aboutKids: Lucy Locket loses her little purse, and her friend Kitty Fisher finds it. The purse was empty, except for a pretty ribbon.
lucy-locket.story: James Orchard Halliwell recorded the rhyme in 1842, though it was already popular in Britain and America. The name Lucy Lockit appears in John Gay's The Beggar's Opera (1728). It is often sung to the tune of Yankee Doodle, and teachers use a simple three-note playground chant for it.
lucy-locket.funFact: A pocket used to be a separate little pouch tied around the waist under a skirt, so it really could get lost.
lucy-locket.myth: The rhyme is often said to be about two real, famous 18th-century London women who were rivals. Halliwell suggested this, but no evidence has been found that the rhyme describes real people.

mary-had-a-little-lamb.writtenBy: Words: Sarah Josepha Hale. Tune: traditional American (shared with the chorus of 'Goodnight, Ladies')
mary-had-a-little-lamb.aboutKids: Mary has a fluffy little lamb who loves her so much that it follows her all the way to school.
mary-had-a-little-lamb.story: Sarah Josepha Hale published the poem in Poems for Our Children (Boston, 1830). Lowell Mason set it to music in the 1830s, but that tune has fallen out of use. Today it is sung to the melody of the 'Merrily we roll along' chorus, with repeated phrases added to the verses.
mary-had-a-little-lamb.funFact: In 1877 Thomas Edison recited this rhyme into his new phonograph, the first words ever recorded on it.
mary-had-a-little-lamb.myth: Mary Sawyer of Sterling, Massachusetts later said a young man named John Roulstone wrote the first verse after her lamb came to school. No evidence beyond her memory supports this; the earliest records support Hale as author.

merrily-we-roll-along.writtenBy: Traditional American; linked to 'Goodnight, Ladies', whose earliest form is credited to E. P. Christy
merrily-we-roll-along.aboutKids: Friends roll happily along together, over the hills and far away, singing as they go.
merrily-we-roll-along.story: The song grew out of 'Goodnight, Ladies'. Its earliest form, 'Farewell, Ladies', was printed in 1847 and credited to E. P. Christy, whose touring troupe likely sang it to close their shows. The full song, including the rolling-along chorus, was first published in 1867.
merrily-we-roll-along.funFact: Its tune is the same one most children now use to sing Mary Had a Little Lamb.

one-two-buckle-my-shoe.origin: England (also early in the United States)
one-two-buckle-my-shoe.aboutKids: A counting rhyme that goes from one to ten while a child buckles shoes, knocks on a door and picks up sticks.
one-two-buckle-my-shoe.story: The rhyme was first printed in Songs for the Nursery, published in London in 1805, but is probably much older. No author is known. It was made to help small children learn to count, and Victorian artist Walter Crane later illustrated it in popular picture books.
one-two-buckle-my-shoe.funFact: An elderly woman told a folklorist that children in Wrentham, Massachusetts used a longer version of this rhyme as early as 1780.

pease-porridge-hot.aboutKids: A clapping game about a pot of pea porridge. Some like it hot, some like it cold, and some like it old.
pease-porridge-hot.story: Its origins are unknown. The earliest known version is a riddle in John Newbery's Mother Goose's Melody, from around the 1760s. Pease porridge, now called pease pudding, is a thick dish of boiled split peas. Children pair up and clap hands, thighs and each other's palms in time with the words.
pease-porridge-hot.funFact: Long ago 'pease' meant the food itself, like 'oatmeal'. The words 'pea' and 'peas' came later.

a-tisket-a-tasket.aboutKids: A child carries a little green and yellow basket with a letter inside, then drops it on the way.
a-tisket-a-tasket.story: The rhyme was first noted in the United States in 1879 as a circle game: one child walks around the outside of the ring, drops a handkerchief behind someone, and gets chased. In 1938 Ella Fitzgerald and Al Feldman (Van Alexander) turned it into a swing hit with Chick Webb's orchestra.
a-tisket-a-tasket.funFact: Ella Fitzgerald was just 21 when her version of this playground rhyme became her first million-selling record.

oh-where-has-my-little-dog-gone.writtenBy: Words: Septimus Winner. Tune: German folk song 'Zu Lauterbach'
oh-where-has-my-little-dog-gone.aboutKids: Someone has lost their little puppy and looks everywhere, wondering where the dog could be.
oh-where-has-my-little-dog-gone.story: Philadelphia songwriter Septimus Winner published 'Der Deitcher's Dog' in 1864, a comic song written in a German-American accent and set to the German folk tune 'Zu Lauterbach'. It sold very well in his lifetime, and its first verse later became a much-loved nursery song.
oh-where-has-my-little-dog-gone.funFact: Winner also wrote songs as 'Alice Hawthorne', a pen name taken from his mother's family, who were related to author Nathaniel Hawthorne.

polly-put-the-kettle-on.year: 1803 (first print, as 'Molly Put the Kettle On'); 1841 (modern words)
polly-put-the-kettle-on.origin: England (early prints also in Dublin and New York)
polly-put-the-kettle-on.aboutKids: Polly puts the kettle on so everyone can have tea, and her sister Sukey takes it off again.
polly-put-the-kettle-on.story: Joseph Dale published it in London in 1803 as 'Molly Put the Kettle On', to a tune known since the 1770s. Versions with Polly were printed in Dublin and New York in the same years. Its modern words were first recorded in Charles Dickens' novel Barnaby Rudge (1841). Polly was a pet name for Mary.
polly-put-the-kettle-on.funFact: In Barnaby Rudge, a talking raven named Grip calls out this rhyme. Dickens kept a real pet raven, also named Grip.

skip-to-my-lou.aboutKids: Friends skip around in a circle, holding hands and swapping partners, laughing and dancing as they go.
skip-to-my-lou.story: Skip to My Lou was a play-party song from the American frontier. Where dancing to instruments was frowned upon for religious reasons, young people sang and played ring games instead. Couples skipped in a circle while one player in the middle chose a new partner. Folklorists John and Alan Lomax called it an ice-breaker.
skip-to-my-lou.funFact: The 'lou' in the title probably comes from the Scottish word 'loo', which means love.

the-muffin-man.aboutKids: A friendly question game: do you know the muffin man who lives on Drury Lane and brings fresh muffins to the door?
the-muffin-man.story: The song was first recorded in a British manuscript around 1820, now in Oxford's Bodleian Library. Muffin men really existed: street sellers brought bread-like English muffins door to door in 19th-century London. Children have played it as a question-and-answer game, a guessing game and a ring dance.
the-muffin-man.funFact: In the Dutch version, the muffin man becomes a mussel man, and Drury Lane becomes a fishing harbour near The Hague.
the-muffin-man.myth: An internet story claims the song warned children about a dangerous baker named Frederick Thomas Lynwood. Snopes and Mental Floss found no record he existed; the tale traces to a parody website.

are-you-sleeping.writtenBy: Traditional French round; music sometimes attributed to Jean-Philippe Rameau (unproven). English words traditional
are-you-sleeping.aboutKids: Brother John is still fast asleep in bed, so everyone sings to wake him up because the morning bells are ringing.
are-you-sleeping.story: A French round about a sleepy friar who should be ringing the bells for early prayers. Its earliest known source is a French manuscript of about 1775-1785, where it is titled Frere Blaise; it was first printed in 1811. A scholar has found evidence linking the music to Rameau, but authorship is unproven.
are-you-sleeping.funFact: Composer Gustav Mahler turned the tune into a slow, minor-key march in the third movement of his First Symphony.
are-you-sleeping.myth: A claim that the song is about the 17th-century surgeon Frere Jacques Beaulieu has no supporting evidence. Who wrote the round, and why, is unknown.

here-we-go-looby-loo.aboutKids: Children hold hands in a circle and skip around, then put a hand, a foot or their head in the middle and shake it.
here-we-go-looby-loo.story: A traditional circle game in which players put in and shake each body part in turn. The Opies found the dance known by 1745; Robert Chambers printed a text in The Popular Rhymes of Scotland, and Alice Gomme recorded versions in 1894. It spread to America, Ireland and New Zealand, and may be an ancestor of the Hokey Pokey.
here-we-go-looby-loo.funFact: Looby Loo was the name of a singing rag doll in the BBC puppet show Andy Pandy, first broadcast in 1950.

little-bo-peep.writtenBy: Traditional English nursery rhyme. Tune: traditional, first printed by J. W. Elliott (1870)
little-bo-peep.aboutKids: Little Bo-Peep cannot find her sheep anywhere. She learns that if she waits patiently, they will wander home all by themselves.
little-bo-peep.story: An English nursery rhyme. A manuscript of about 1805 holds the first verse, and the fuller version was printed in Gammer Gurton's Garland in 1810. Bo-peep, an old name for peekaboo, is centuries older than the rhyme. The familiar tune was first printed by James William Elliott in 1870.
little-bo-peep.funFact: Bo-peep, the old English name for peekaboo, was already played in Shakespeare's time; he mentions it in King Lear.
little-bo-peep.myth: Hidden meanings have been proposed (the English Civil War, the Jacobites, Mary Queen of Scots, smuggling), but none is proven, and the rhyme is not recorded before about 1805.

this-old-man.aboutKids: A cheerful old man counts all the way from one to ten, tapping out a rhythm on something new for every number.
this-old-man.story: A traditional counting song that began as a children's singing game. Folk-song scholar Anne Gilchrist remembered a version learned from her Welsh nurse in the 1870s. Baring-Gould and Sharp printed a version in English Folk-Songs for Schools (1906), and Malcolm Arnold's arrangement for a 1958 film turned it into a pop hit.
this-old-man.funFact: The Barney theme song I Love You is sung to this same old tune.

all-the-pretty-little-horses.writtenBy: Traditional African American lullaby (Southern United States)
all-the-pretty-little-horses.aboutKids: A grown-up gently rocks a little one to sleep, promising lovely horses of every color to play with in the morning.
all-the-pretty-little-horses.story: A traditional lullaby from the American South, widely believed to be of African American origin. Its earliest known printing is in Maud Lindsay's 1903 kindergarten story A White Dove, which calls it an old lullaby. Dorothy Scarborough found it widely sung across the South in 1925, and John and Alan Lomax published it in 1934.
all-the-pretty-little-horses.funFact: Its first known printing was tucked inside a 1903 story for kindergarten children by Maud Lindsay, an Alabama teacher.
all-the-pretty-little-horses.myth: It is often described as a lullaby sung by enslaved women to the white children in their care, as Scarborough (1925) and others wrote. This is plausible, but no 19th-century record survives to confirm it.

did-you-ever-see-a-lassie.writtenBy: Words: traditional singing game. Tune: Austrian folk song O du lieber Augustin
did-you-ever-see-a-lassie.aboutKids: One child in the circle does a silly move, everyone else copies it, and then someone new gets a turn to lead.
did-you-ever-see-a-lassie.story: A singing game in which a leader acts out a motion and the circle copies it. The tune is the Viennese song O du lieber Augustin, first published around 1800. Despite the Scottish words lassie and laddie, the game was first collected in the United States in the 1890s; a print appears in Jessie Bancroft's Games for the Playground (1909).
did-you-ever-see-a-lassie.funFact: Despite its Scottish-sounding words, the game was first written down in America and was not found in Britain until the mid-1900s.
did-you-ever-see-a-lassie.myth: It is often called a Scottish folk song because of the words lassie and laddie, but it was collected in the US first. The story that the tune is about the Viennese bagpiper Marx Augustin (1679) is a legend.

hickory-dickory-dock.writtenBy: Traditional English nursery rhyme. Tune: J. W. Elliott (1870)
hickory-dickory-dock.aboutKids: A little mouse scampers up a tall clock. When the clock strikes one, he gets a surprise and scurries back down.
hickory-dickory-dock.story: First printed in Tommy Thumb's Pretty Song Book (London, 1744), the first collection of English nursery rhymes, spelled Hickere Dickere Dock. The nonsense opening may come from counting-out games; some link it to old Westmorland shepherds' words for eight, nine and ten. The usual tune was published by J. W. Elliott in 1870.
hickory-dickory-dock.funFact: Exeter Cathedral's clock door has had a cat-sized hole since 1598, so the cathedral cat could slip in and chase mice.
hickory-dickory-dock.myth: The rhyme is often said to be about Exeter Cathedral's astronomical clock and its cat door. The cat door is real, but no evidence links it to the rhyme.

pop-goes-the-weasel.writtenBy: Traditional English dance tune; earliest sheet music Jullien & Co. (1853), arranged by George Thompson
pop-goes-the-weasel.aboutKids: A playful weasel and a cheeky monkey dash round and round, and everyone waits for the big pop at the end!
pop-goes-the-weasel.story: It began as a fashionable social dance that swept England in late 1852; dancers sang the title line while ducking under each other's arms. The earliest known sheet music, from Jullien & Co., dates from 1853, and American editions followed that year. Words were added around 1854-55, and the verses kept changing for decades.
pop-goes-the-weasel.funFact: Before it was a nursery song, it was a grown-up dance craze in 1852, taught in dance schools and played at fancy balls.
pop-goes-the-weasel.myth: The popular claim that weasel is Cockney rhyming slang for coat (weasel and stoat), so the song is about pawning a coat, is unproven. That slang is documented only from the 1930s, and in the 1850s nobody seemed to know what the line meant.

sing-a-song-of-sixpence.writtenBy: Traditional English nursery rhyme. Tune: traditional, in J. W. Elliott (1870)
sing-a-song-of-sixpence.aboutKids: A king and queen sit down to a special pie, and when it is opened, a whole flock of blackbirds starts to sing!
sing-a-song-of-sixpence.story: The first verse appeared in Tommy Thumb's Pretty Song Book (London, 1744), though with a different filling than blackbirds. A version with birds was printed around 1780, the four-verse rhyme by 1784, and happier extra endings were added in the 1800s. Possible earlier allusions in Shakespeare and in Beaumont and Fletcher are uncertain.
sing-a-song-of-sixpence.funFact: Birds in a pie were a real party trick: a 1549 Italian cookbook explains how to bake a pie so live birds fly out.
sing-a-song-of-sixpence.myth: The claim that the pirate Blackbeard used the rhyme as a secret recruiting code is false; Snopes invented it in 1999 as a deliberate spoof. Other hidden meanings (Henry VIII, the calendar) are unproven.

the-grand-old-duke-of-york.aboutKids: A duke leads ten thousand marching soldiers all the way up a big hill, and then all the way back down again.
the-grand-old-duke-of-york.story: Its oldest relative is Old Tarlton's Song, printed in 1642 and credited to the Elizabethan clown Richard Tarlton, about a King of France marching his army up a hill. A Duke of York version was noted in Warwickshire in 1892, and the modern words were printed in Arthur Rackham's Mother Goose (1913). It is a favorite action song.
the-grand-old-duke-of-york.funFact: The oldest known version, from 1642, was about a King of France, not a duke, and his army was even bigger.
the-grand-old-duke-of-york.myth: The duke is often said to be Prince Frederick, Duke of York, in the 1793-94 Flanders campaign, or Richard, Duke of York, in 1460. No evidence links the rhyme to either.

go-tell-aunt-rhody.writtenBy: Words: Traditional American. Tune: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
go-tell-aunt-rhody.aboutKids: Someone hurries off to tell Aunt Rhody some sad news about her old gray goose, who leaves her little goslings behind.
go-tell-aunt-rhody.story: The melody began as a wordless dance in Jean-Jacques Rousseau's 1752 opera Le devin du village. It spread through Britain and America, became the hymn tune Greenville around 1825, and was later sung with American folk words about Aunt Rhody's goose. Folklorists, including Cecil Sharp, collected those words in the early 1900s.
go-tell-aunt-rhody.funFact: The tune was written by Jean-Jacques Rousseau, the famous French philosopher, as a dance in his 1752 opera.
go-tell-aunt-rhody.myth: The tune is often called Rousseau's Dream, as if it came to him in a dream. The name comes from J. B. Cramer's piano variations and a mix-up with a different Rousseau piece.

hot-cross-buns.aboutKids: Long ago in London, sellers walked the streets calling out about warm, sweet buns with a cross on top, sold for just a penny.
hot-cross-buns.story: It began as a London street cry: sellers called out to sell spiced buns on Good Friday, when shops were shut, a cry recorded in Poor Robin's Almanack in 1733. The words appeared as a round in the London Chronicle in 1767 and in the Christmas Box in 1798. Today it is often a child's first tune.
hot-cross-buns.funFact: The artist Thomas Rowlandson drew a London bun seller calling out this very cry in a 1799 print, now in the London Museum.
hot-cross-buns.myth: A popular story says a monk in St Albans baked the first cross buns in 1361. There is no evidence for it, and the name hot cross buns is first recorded in 1733.

lightly-row.writtenBy: Tune: traditional German folk melody (Hanschen klein). English words: anonymous
lightly-row.year: 1784 or earlier (tune); English words printed by 1914
lightly-row.aboutKids: A family glides along in a little boat, rowing gently over calm, sparkly water on a bright, sunny day.
lightly-row.story: The melody is an old German folk tune: the earliest evidence is a dance tune written down in 1784, and Franz Wiedemann's words Hanschen klein (1860) made it a German children's favorite. American school songbooks set English boating words, Lightly Row, to it; one version appears in Hollis Dann's First Year Music (1914).
lightly-row.funFact: Lightly Row is one of the very first pieces in the Suzuki violin method, coming right after Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star.

spring-vivaldi.writtenBy: Antonio Vivaldi (music); English words by Little Duet
spring-vivaldi.aboutKids: Spring is here! Birds sing, a little storm rumbles past, and then the birds start singing again, played by happy violins.
spring-vivaldi.story: Spring is the first of Vivaldi's four violin concertos known as The Four Seasons, composed around 1718-1720 and published in Amsterdam in 1725 in his collection Il cimento dell'armonia e dell'inventione. Each concerto comes with a sonnet, possibly by Vivaldi himself, describing the scenes the music paints, an early example of storytelling in music.
spring-vivaldi.funFact: In Spring, the violins imitate singing birds, and the music follows a poem line by line, even pausing for a thunderstorm.

william-tell-overture.aboutKids: Fast, bouncy music that sounds like horses galloping. Trumpets call, and the whole orchestra races to an exciting finish!
william-tell-overture.story: Rossini wrote the overture for Guillaume Tell, his last opera, which premiered in Paris in 1829 and tells the Swiss legend of William Tell. The overture has four parts played without a break; the famous final gallop is known as the March of the Swiss Soldiers. Rossini lived 39 more years without writing another opera.
william-tell-overture.funFact: The gallop became the theme music of The Lone Ranger on radio and TV, so many people picture a cowboy riding to the rescue.
william-tell-overture.myth: The finale is widely heard as a cavalry charge or horse race, but the opera has no horses or cavalry in it; the section is the March of the Swiss Soldiers.

moonlight-au-clair-de-la-lune.writtenBy: Traditional French folk song; English words by Little Duet
moonlight-au-clair-de-la-lune.aboutKids: Under the bright moon, a friend knocks on a neighbor's door to ask for a pen and a little light.
moonlight-au-clair-de-la-lune.story: An 18th-century French folk song whose writer is unknown. The earliest printing found is from 1820, and fuller versions appeared in French song collections in 1858 and 1870. Its gentle, simple tune has made it a favorite first piece for beginners, and composers from Clementi to Debussy and Satie have borrowed it.
moonlight-au-clair-de-la-lune.funFact: In 1860, French inventor Edouard-Leon Scott de Martinville recorded himself singing it: the oldest known recording of a recognizable human voice.
moonlight-au-clair-de-la-lune.myth: When the 1860 recording was first played back in 2008, many reports said a young girl was singing. It had been played at double speed; at the right speed, it is almost certainly Scott himself.

camptown-races.aboutKids: Horses race round and round a long track all day and all night, while the crowd cheers and everyone sings along.
camptown-races.story: Stephen Foster wrote it in 1850 for the minstrel stage, and F. D. Benteen of Baltimore published it that February as Gwine to Run All Night, or De Camptown Races. Christy's Minstrels made it a nationwide hit. Its original lyrics were written in a stereotyped dialect; modern versions use standard words.
camptown-races.funFact: Camptown may be a real village in Pennsylvania that Foster knew from his school days nearby.

jolly-old-saint-nicholas.writtenBy: Words: Emily Huntington Miller (adapted from her poem). Music: James R. Murray
jolly-old-saint-nicholas.aboutKids: A child whispers a secret Christmas wish to Santa Claus, hoping for special presents to be left while everyone is asleep.
jolly-old-saint-nicholas.story: The words grew from Lilly's Secret, a poem by Emily Huntington Miller in the children's magazine The Little Corporal in December 1865. The tune is credited to American composer James R. Murray and was published in School Chimes (1874). The song in its familiar form was printed in 1881 and has been a Christmas favorite ever since.
jolly-old-saint-nicholas.funFact: The song began as a poem called Lilly's Secret in a children's magazine, published in December 1865.
jolly-old-saint-nicholas.myth: The words are sometimes credited to Benjamin Hanby, who wrote the similar Up on the Housetop, or to John Piersol McCaskey; the evidence points to Emily Huntington Miller.

michael-row-the-boat.origin: St. Helena Island, South Carolina Sea Islands
michael-row-the-boat.aboutKids: Friends row a boat across the water together, pulling their oars in time and singing to help them reach the shore.
michael-row-the-boat.story: Charles Pickard Ware wrote it down during the Civil War on St. Helena Island, South Carolina, where freedpeople sang it while rowing; his cousin William Francis Allen heard it on Station Creek in 1863. It was published in Slave Songs of the United States (1867). Tony Saletan's 1954 adaptation spread it through the folk revival.
michael-row-the-boat.funFact: In 1961 a folk group called The Highwaymen took the song to number one in both the United States and Britain.
michael-row-the-boat.myth: Pete Seeger is often thought to have written or arranged the modern version; he learned it from Tony Saletan in 1954 and credited him.

morning-mood.writtenBy: Edvard Grieg (music); English words by Little Duet
morning-mood.aboutKids: The sun slowly rises and the music grows brighter and brighter, like a big, sleepy yawn and stretch at the start of the day.
morning-mood.story: Grieg wrote it in 1875 as part of his music for Henrik Ibsen's play Peer Gynt, which premiered in Christiania (now Oslo) on 24 February 1876. It is the prelude to Act IV, and Grieg later made it the opening movement of his Peer Gynt Suite No. 1, published in 1888.
morning-mood.funFact: It sounds like a Norwegian sunrise, but in the play it is a dawn in the desert of Morocco.
morning-mood.myth: It is often thought to picture a sunrise over Norway's fjords; in Ibsen's play it accompanies a desert dawn in Morocco, where Peer Gynt is stranded.

oh-dear-what-can-the-matter-be.aboutKids: Someone is waiting and waiting for Johnny to come home from the busy fair, and wonders what is taking him so long.
oh-dear-what-can-the-matter-be.story: No author is known. A manuscript version dates from the 1770s, and the song was first printed in London in The British Lyre (1792). It was sung at London concerts, appeared in Scottish and Irish collections, and crossed to America within a decade. Its bouncy tune became more famous than its words.
oh-dear-what-can-the-matter-be.funFact: It reached America so soon after independence that many Americans grew up thinking it was an American song.

alouette.origin: Canada (Quebec), possibly with roots in France
alouette.aboutKids: Alouette is the French word for a lark, a small brown bird that sings while it flies high up in the sky.
alouette.story: Nobody knows who made it up. It was first printed in 1879 in a songbook for students of McGill College in Montreal, and the first known French printing came in 1893. Allied soldiers learned it in France during the First World War and carried it home, and it became a worldwide symbol of French Canada.
alouette.funFact: Montreal's professional football team, the Alouettes, is named after this song.
alouette.myth: Often said to be a paddling song of the voyageurs, the French-Canadian fur-trade canoeists. That link is a popular theory, not documented; folklorist Marius Barbeau thought the song came from France. The earliest known printing is the 1879 McGill songbook.

ode-to-joy.writtenBy: Music: Ludwig van Beethoven. English words: Little Duet
ode-to-joy.aboutKids: A big, bright, happy tune about joy, that warm feeling when everyone sings together and feels glad inside.
ode-to-joy.story: This is the main theme from the finale of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony, first performed in Vienna on 7 May 1824 and printed by Schott in 1826. In the symphony, a choir sings Friedrich Schiller's 1785 poem An die Freude (To Joy). Beethoven was almost completely deaf when he wrote it.
ode-to-joy.funFact: At the premiere Beethoven could not hear the cheering, so a singer gently turned him around to see the audience clapping.
ode-to-joy.myth: A popular story says CDs were made 74 minutes long so Beethoven's Ninth would fit. Philips engineer Kees Immink recalled that a long recording of the Ninth was used to justify the length after it had largely been settled, so the symphony was not the real reason.

oh-susanna.aboutKids: A traveller plays his banjo and journeys a long, long way to visit his good friend Susanna.
oh-susanna.story: Stephen Foster wrote it in his early twenties; it was first sung in Pittsburgh in 1847 and published in Cincinnati in 1848. Foster was paid just 100 dollars, while dozens of other publishers printed copies of their own. Sheet music sales passed 100,000, a record for an American song at the time.
oh-susanna.funFact: Gold seekers heading to California in 1849 sang it so often, with new words about their journey, that it became their unofficial theme song.

sur-le-pont-davignon.writtenBy: Traditional French song. English words: Little Duet
sur-le-pont-davignon.aboutKids: People hold hands and dance round and round in a circle beside a very old stone bridge in a French town called Avignon.
sur-le-pont-davignon.story: No one knows who wrote it. Some scholars think it goes back to the 15th century, but the evidence is thin. It became famous across France in 1853, when composer Adolphe Adam used it in his comic opera Le Sourd ou l'Auberge pleine. The song is about the Saint-Benezet bridge, finished in 1185.
sur-le-pont-davignon.funFact: The real bridge once had 22 arches across the river Rhone. Floods washed most away, and today only 4 remain, stopping in mid-river.
sur-le-pont-davignon.myth: People are often imagined dancing on the bridge itself, but it was too narrow for that; dances are thought to have taken place on the riverbanks below, which is why some older singers say 'sous' (under) rather than 'sur' (on).

over-the-river-and-through-the-wood.writtenBy: Words: Lydia Maria Child. Tune: traditional American, composer unknown
over-the-river-and-through-the-wood.aboutKids: A family rides in a horse-drawn sleigh over the river and through the snowy woods to their grandparents' house for a holiday dinner.
over-the-river-and-through-the-wood.story: Lydia Maria Child, a writer and campaigner, published the poem in 1844 as The New-England Boy's Song about Thanksgiving Day in her book Flowers for Children. It recalls childhood trips to her grandparents' house in Medford, Massachusetts. Nobody knows who set it to music, but it was a classroom favourite by 1900.
over-the-river-and-through-the-wood.funFact: Child's original poem goes to grandfather's house, not grandmother's. The house in Medford, Massachusetts, still stands today.

shoo-fly-dont-bother-me.writtenBy: Words credited to Billy Reeves, music to Frank Campbell (1869 sheet music); also claimed by T. Brigham Bishop
shoo-fly-dont-bother-me.aboutKids: A buzzy little fly keeps zooming around, and we wave our hands and ask it nicely to fly away.
shoo-fly-dont-bother-me.story: The song became a hit on the American stage in 1869. One 1869 sheet music edition credits Billy Reeves for the words and Frank Campbell for the music, arranged by Rollin Howard; T. Brigham Bishop published his own edition the same year and claimed he wrote it. Who really wrote it remains unsettled.
shoo-fly-dont-bother-me.funFact: Its 1869 sheet music described it as a comic song and dance, or walk around.
shoo-fly-dont-bother-me.myth: T. Brigham Bishop said he wrote the song during the Civil War, inspired by a remark from a soldier in his company. This is his own account and has never been independently confirmed.

up-on-the-housetop.aboutKids: Santa's reindeer land softly on the roof, and Santa slides down the chimney with a sack full of toys for the children.
up-on-the-housetop.story: Benjamin Hanby wrote it in late 1864 in New Paris, Ohio, for the children in his singing school, because he could not afford printed music. It was published in 1866 by Root and Cady of Chicago in a children's songbook. Hanby died in 1867, aged 33, and was long forgotten as its author.
up-on-the-housetop.funFact: It is thought to be the first Christmas song mainly about Santa Claus, and the second-oldest non-religious Christmas song after Jingle Bells.

all-through-the-night.writtenBy: Tune: traditional Welsh. English words: Harold Boulton
all-through-the-night.aboutKids: A soft, sleepy lullaby that promises a little one they will be cosy, loved and looked after all night long.
all-through-the-night.story: The Welsh melody Ar Hyd y Nos was first printed in 1784 by Edward Jones, harpist to the Prince of Wales, in his Musical and Poetical Relicks of the Welsh Bards. Sir Harold Boulton wrote the best-known English words in 1884. The Welsh words most sung today are by the poet John Ceiriog Hughes.
all-through-the-night.funFact: The Welsh title, Ar Hyd y Nos, means exactly the same as the English one: all through the night.

o-christmas-tree.writtenBy: Words: Ernst Anschutz (after August Zarnack). Tune: traditional German. English words: traditional and Little Duet
o-christmas-tree.aboutKids: We sing to a fir tree whose needles stay green and fresh all winter long, even when snow is everywhere.
o-christmas-tree.story: It began as an old German folk song about a fir tree, praised for staying green all year. In 1820 teacher August Zarnack printed a version, and in 1824 Leipzig teacher and organist Ernst Anschutz kept its first verse and added new verses linking the tree to Christmas. It is a Christmas song sung for 200 years.
o-christmas-tree.funFact: Researchers think it may be the very first song to connect the fir tree with Christmas.

surprise-symphony.writtenBy: Music: Joseph Haydn. English words: Little Duet
surprise-symphony.origin: London, England (composed by an Austrian composer)
surprise-symphony.aboutKids: A quiet, tiptoeing tune creeps along softly, and then suddenly goes BOOM with one big loud chord. Are you ready for the surprise?
surprise-symphony.story: Haydn wrote Symphony No. 94 in London in 1791, during his first visit to England, and led its premiere at the Hanover Square Rooms on 23 March 1792. The gentle slow movement is famous for a sudden loud chord, which gave the whole symphony its nickname, the Surprise.
surprise-symphony.funFact: Haydn liked this tune so much that he reused it years later in The Seasons, where a farmer whistles it while ploughing.
surprise-symphony.myth: The loud chord is often said to have been written to wake up sleeping listeners. When his biographer Griesinger asked, Haydn said no: he simply wanted to surprise the public with something new and make a brilliant debut.

the-bear-went-over-the-mountain.writtenBy: Words: traditional American. Tune: traditional French ('Malbrough s'en va-t-en guerre')
the-bear-went-over-the-mountain.aboutKids: A curious bear climbs all the way over a big mountain to find out what is on the other side. What might he see?
the-bear-went-over-the-mountain.story: The words are traditional and nobody knows who made them up. They are sung to the tune of For He's a Jolly Good Fellow, which comes from the French song Malbrough s'en va-t-en guerre. That tune swept France in the 1780s and later travelled to Britain and America.
the-bear-went-over-the-mountain.funFact: In 1781 a nurse sang this tune while rocking the French royal baby, and Queen Marie Antoinette liked it so much she sang it too.

twelve-days-of-christmas.writtenBy: Words: traditional English. Familiar tune: arranged by Frederic Austin
twelve-days-of-christmas.aboutKids: A friend gives a lovely present for the first day of Christmas: a plump little partridge bird sitting in a pear tree.
twelve-days-of-christmas.story: The words first appeared in Mirth without Mischief, a London children's book from about 1780, as a memory-and-forfeits game: each player repeated the growing list, and a mistake cost a forfeit such as a kiss or a sweet. The tune most people know was arranged by English singer Frederic Austin and published in 1909.
twelve-days-of-christmas.funFact: Children once played it as a memory game. Anyone who forgot a gift had to pay a forfeit, often a kiss or a sweet.
twelve-days-of-christmas.myth: A popular claim says the song was a secret code teaching Catholic beliefs in hiding. Snopes finds no evidence: the claim appears only in the late 20th century, and the supposed meanings were beliefs Catholics and Protestants shared.

three-blind-mice.writtenBy: Traditional English round, first printed by Thomas Ravenscroft
three-blind-mice.aboutKids: Three little mice scurry and scamper together, running here and there as fast as their tiny feet can go.
three-blind-mice.story: It was first printed in 1609 as a round for three voices in Thomas Ravenscroft's songbook Deuteromelia; Ravenscroft may have written it himself. The early words were quite different from today's. The rhyme entered children's books in 1842, and today's familiar words took shape over the following decades.
three-blind-mice.funFact: Printed in 1609, it is called the earliest printed non-religious song that is still widely known today.
three-blind-mice.myth: A popular claim says the rhyme secretly describes Queen Mary I and three Protestant bishops. There is no evidence: the bishops were not blinded, the rhyme was first printed decades after her reign, and the earliest words do not match the story.

shell-be-coming-round-the-mountain.aboutKids: Someone special is coming to visit, riding all the way around the mountain, and everyone gets ready to cheer and say hello.
shell-be-coming-round-the-mountain.story: It grew out of the spiritual When the Chariot Comes, printed in 1899. Poet Carl Sandburg reported that railroad workers in the Midwest sang new words to the melody in the 1890s, and he printed that version in his 1927 collection The American Songbag. Families have kept adding funny verses ever since.
shell-be-coming-round-the-mountain.funFact: The first recordings were made in 1924 and 1925 by country singers Henry Whitter and Vernon Dalhart.

good-king-wenceslas.writtenBy: Words: John Mason Neale. Tune: 'Tempus adest floridum', traditional
good-king-wenceslas.origin: England (tune from the Piae Cantiones collection)
good-king-wenceslas.aboutKids: A kind king looks out at the deep snow, sees a poor man gathering sticks, and goes out to bring him food and warmth.
good-king-wenceslas.story: John Mason Neale wrote the words in 1853 for Carols for Christmas-tide, edited with Thomas Helmore. They borrowed the tune from a medieval spring song, Tempus adest floridum, printed in the 1582 songbook Piae Cantiones. The carol, sung for over 170 years, is set on St Stephen's Day, 26 December.
good-king-wenceslas.funFact: The tune comes from Piae Cantiones, a 1582 songbook compiled by the headmaster of Turku Cathedral School in Finland.
good-king-wenceslas.myth: The carol calls him a king, but the real Wenceslas (c. 907-935) was Duke of Bohemia, known for his charity. The royal title was granted after his death by Emperor Otto I.

cockles-and-mussels-molly-malone.writtenBy: Attributed to James Yorkston (1884 London edition); otherwise traditional
cockles-and-mussels-molly-malone.origin: Ireland (Dublin setting); first printed in the USA and Britain
cockles-and-mussels-molly-malone.aboutKids: Molly pushes her wheelbarrow through the streets of Dublin, calling out to everyone that she has fresh cockles and mussels to sell.
cockles-and-mussels-molly-malone.story: The song is set in Dublin, but its earliest known printing was in Boston in 1876, in a student songbook. In 1884 a London publisher issued it as a comic song by James Yorkston of Edinburgh, and a variant appeared in Cambridge, Massachusetts the same year. It is now Dublin's unofficial anthem.
cockles-and-mussels-molly-malone.funFact: A statue of Molly with her cart stands on Suffolk Street in Dublin, and visitors love to stop for a photo with her.
cockles-and-mussels-molly-malone.myth: Molly is often said to be a real 17th-century Dublin fishseller. Historians find no evidence; the 1988 'Molly Malone Day' rested on records of a Mary Malone with no proven link to the song.

auld-lang-syne.writtenBy: Words: Robert Burns (from an older song). Tune: traditional Scottish
auld-lang-syne.aboutKids: Old friends hold hands in a big circle and sing together, remembering all the happy times they shared long, long ago.
auld-lang-syne.story: Robert Burns sent the song to the Scots Musical Museum in 1788, calling it an old song, and reworked earlier verses. It was printed in 1796, the year he died, to a slow tune. In 1799 George Thomson matched it with the cheerful melody sung today at New Year around the world.
auld-lang-syne.funFact: In Japan the same tune is played in shops and restaurants to tell customers it is nearly closing time.
auld-lang-syne.myth: It is often treated as wholly Burns's own poem. He reshaped an older song (a 1711 version already had a similar verse and chorus), and his story of taking it down from an old man's singing may have been his own invention.

daisy-bell.aboutKids: Someone sings to their friend Daisy, hoping she will ride with them on a special bicycle with two seats, one behind the other.
daisy-bell.story: Harry Dacre, the pen name of Frank Dean from the Isle of Man, took a bicycle to America in 1891 and paid import duty on it. A friend joked that a bicycle built for two would have cost double, and Dacre put the phrase into his song. It became a London music hall hit in 1892.
daisy-bell.funFact: In 1961 an IBM computer at Bell Labs sang this song, one of the first songs ever sung by a computer.
daisy-bell.myth: It is often said Dacre wrote it about Daisy Greville, Countess of Warwick. This is a popular claim with no firm evidence.

eine-kleine-nachtmusik.aboutKids: A bright, bouncy piece played by violins and other string instruments. Its German name means a little night music.
eine-kleine-nachtmusik.story: Mozart finished this serenade for strings in Vienna on 10 August 1787, while also working on his opera Don Giovanni. Nobody knows why he wrote it or whether it was played in his lifetime. His widow Constanze sold the manuscript, and it was published around 1827, more than 30 years after his death.
eine-kleine-nachtmusik.funFact: Mozart's own list says the piece had five movements, but one went missing long ago, so we play only four.

home-on-the-range.writtenBy: Words: Brewster M. Higley. Music: Daniel E. Kelley
home-on-the-range.aboutKids: A happy song about a cozy home on wide, open grassland, with buffalo, deer and antelope nearby and big, clear skies above.
home-on-the-range.story: Brewster Higley, a doctor homesteading in Kansas, wrote the poem 'My Western Home' in the early 1870s, and his friend Daniel Kelley set it to music. Cowboys and settlers carried it west. When a 1934 lawsuit claimed the song, investigators traced it back to Higley. Kansas made it the state song in 1947.
home-on-the-range.funFact: Higley's little log cabin in Kansas, where the song was written, still stands and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

joy-to-the-world.writtenBy: Words: Isaac Watts. Tune: 'Antioch', arranged by Lowell Mason
joy-to-the-world.aboutKids: A bright, bouncy Christmas song that invites the whole wide world, the fields, hills and seas, to sing and celebrate together.
joy-to-the-world.story: Isaac Watts wrote the words in 1719 as a retelling of Psalm 98 in his book The Psalms of David Imitated; it was not written specifically for Christmas. American music teacher Lowell Mason matched it with the tune 'Antioch' in the 1830s, and the pairing became a Christmas favorite in North America.
joy-to-the-world.funFact: It is the most-published Christmas hymn in North America, appearing in more than 1,300 hymnals.
joy-to-the-world.myth: Often said to be by Handel. The tune has never been found in Handel's works; Mason labelled it 'arranged from Handel' because a few phrases resemble Messiah, but scholars treat it as Mason's own arrangement of an American tune.

my-bonnie.writtenBy: Traditional; first published by Charles E. Pratt (as H. J. Fuller)
my-bonnie.origin: Uncertain; British Isles roots, popularized in the United States
my-bonnie.aboutKids: Someone misses a dear friend who sailed far away across the big blue ocean, and wishes with all their heart they would come home.
my-bonnie.story: Nobody knows who first wrote it. Shoppers were asking for it in music stores in the 1870s, so Charles E. Pratt published it in 1881 as 'Bring Back My Bonnie to Me' under a pen name. It became a hit with college singing groups, and may grow from an 1860s stage song, 'My Barney Lies over the Ocean'.
my-bonnie.funFact: In 1961 the Beatles recorded it in Hamburg backing singer Tony Sheridan, one of their very first records.
my-bonnie.myth: Often said to be a secret song about Bonnie Prince Charlie after 1746. This is only a guess: no early source links the song to him, and the first known printing is from 1881.

clementine.writtenBy: Traditional American; credited to Percy Montrose
clementine.aboutKids: A gold miner's daughter named Clementine wears very big shoes, and her sweetheart sings about how much he misses his darling.
clementine.story: The familiar version was published in Boston in 1884 and credited to Percy Montrose, about whom nothing else is known. An 1863 song with similar words but a different tune came earlier, and another version appeared in 1885. Set in Gold Rush mining country, it became a mock-sad campfire favorite.
clementine.funFact: It was the signature song of the cartoon dog Huckleberry Hound, who sang it in his own wobbly, mixed-up way.

simple-gifts.aboutKids: A gentle, happy song about keeping things simple, being kind, and turning round and round until you land in just the right spot.
simple-gifts.story: Elder Joseph Brackett, a member of the Shakers, a religious community known for plain living, is credited with the song around 1848 in Alfred, Maine. Shakers sang it while dancing. It became famous worldwide after Aaron Copland used it in the 1944 ballet Appalachian Spring.
simple-gifts.funFact: Shaker songbooks call it a quick dance, and the song's words about turning were actually instructions for the dancers' steps.

angels-we-have-heard-on-high.writtenBy: French words and tune: Traditional (anonymous). English words: James Chadwick
angels-we-have-heard-on-high.year: Early 19th century (first printed 1805 or 1842); English words 1860-62
angels-we-have-heard-on-high.aboutKids: In this Christmas carol, shepherds out in the fields hear angels singing high in the sky, and the happy singing echoes over the hills.
angels-we-have-heard-on-high.story: This French carol, 'Les Anges dans nos campagnes', was sung by ordinary people long before anyone knew who wrote it. It was printed in France in the early 1800s. James Chadwick, a Catholic bishop in northern England, wrote the English words around 1860-62, and the carol has been sung across the English-speaking world ever since.
angels-we-have-heard-on-high.funFact: In the chorus, the single word Gloria is stretched across sixteen notes that climb up and tumble down, like a musical rollercoaster.

can-can.writtenBy: Music: Jacques Offenbach. English words: Little Duet
can-can.aboutKids: A super-fast, bouncy dance tune that makes you want to kick your legs up high and spin around until you giggle.
can-can.story: Jacques Offenbach wrote this whirlwind 'Galop infernal' as the closing dance of his comic operetta Orpheus in the Underworld, which opened in Paris in 1858 and was a huge hit. Decades later, Paris dance halls such as the Moulin Rouge adopted it for the high-kicking cancan, and the name stuck.
can-can.funFact: Offenbach never called it the Can-Can. The cancan dance already existed, and the tune only became its theme song years after he died.
can-can.myth: Often said that Offenbach invented the cancan or wrote this as cancan music. The dance began in Paris dance halls in the 1830s, and the tune was linked to it only in the 1890s.

deck-the-halls.writtenBy: Tune: Traditional Welsh ('Nos Galan'). English words: Thomas Oliphant
deck-the-halls.aboutKids: Everyone decorates the house with shiny green holly, gathers around, and sings a cheerful, silly chorus together.
deck-the-halls.story: The tune comes from 'Nos Galan', a Welsh song for New Year's Eve. It appears in an 18th-century manuscript by the harpist John Parry and was printed in 1794. Scottish writer Thomas Oliphant wrote new English words, not a translation, for an 1862 book of Welsh melodies, turning it into a Christmas favorite.
deck-the-halls.funFact: It started as a Welsh New Year's Eve song, and the English title said 'Hall', just one, until about the 1890s.
deck-the-halls.myth: Often said that Mozart used the tune in a violin sonata. This rests on a newspaper column and has not been confirmed; Haydn did arrange the tune in 1803.

fur-elise.writtenBy: Music: Ludwig van Beethoven. English words: Little Duet
fur-elise.aboutKids: A gentle piano tune that rocks back and forth like a little wave, written as a musical gift for a special friend.
fur-elise.story: Beethoven wrote this short piano piece in Vienna in 1810. It was never published in his lifetime: scholar Ludwig Nohl found it and printed it in 1867, forty years after Beethoven died. The manuscript Nohl saw has since been lost, so nobody can check the dedication, and it became one of the world's best-known piano tunes.
fur-elise.funFact: In Taiwan, garbage trucks play Fur Elise as they drive through neighborhoods, so families know it is time to bring out the rubbish.
fur-elise.myth: Often stated as fact that 'Elise' was Therese Malfatti, whose name Nohl misread. This is only one theory; others suggest the singer Elisabeth Rockel, and the manuscript is lost, so Elise's identity is unknown.

greensleeves.aboutKids: A slow, dreamy old tune about a lovely lady who wore a dress with bright green sleeves.
greensleeves.story: In September 1580 a London printer, Richard Jones, registered a ballad called 'A Newe Northen Dittye of ye Ladye Greene Sleves', and the tune quickly became a hit, with more ballads written to it within a year. Shakespeare mentions it in The Merry Wives of Windsor, and in 1865 it became the Christmas carol 'What Child Is This?'
greensleeves.funFact: Shakespeare liked it enough to mention it twice in his comedy The Merry Wives of Windsor, written around 1597.
greensleeves.myth: Often said that King Henry VIII wrote it, sometimes for Anne Boleyn. Henry died in 1547, and the tune is built in an Italian style that reached England only after his death; it first appears in 1580.

hark-the-herald-angels-sing.writtenBy: Words: Charles Wesley (altered by George Whitefield). Music: Felix Mendelssohn, adapted by William H. Cummings
hark-the-herald-angels-sing.aboutKids: A joyful Christmas carol where angels sing happy news across the sky, and everyone on earth joins in the singing.
hark-the-herald-angels-sing.story: Charles Wesley wrote a 'Hymn for Christmas-Day' in 1739, and preacher George Whitefield rewrote its opening in 1753. The tune comes from a piece Felix Mendelssohn wrote in 1840 for a festival in Leipzig. In 1855 English organist William Cummings fitted Wesley's words to Mendelssohn's music, creating the carol sung today.
hark-the-herald-angels-sing.funFact: Mendelssohn wrote the tune to celebrate the 400th anniversary of the printing press, and said it would never suit religious words.

mountain-king.writtenBy: Music: Edvard Grieg. English words: Little Duet
mountain-king.aboutKids: A sneaky tiptoe tune from a fairy-tale mountain hall that starts slow and quiet, then gets faster and louder until everyone is racing.
mountain-king.story: Norwegian composer Edvard Grieg wrote this music in 1875 for Henrik Ibsen's play Peer Gynt, which opened in Christiania (now Oslo) in 1876. It plays when Peer finds himself in the hall of the troll king. The short theme repeats again and again, speeding up each time. Grieg later placed it in his first Peer Gynt Suite (1888).
mountain-king.funFact: Grieg himself did not like it: he wrote that it was so full of cowpats and Norwegian-ness that he could not bear to hear it.

minuet-in-g.writtenBy: Music: Christian Petzold. English words: Little Duet
minuet-in-g.aboutKids: A polite, graceful dance tune, made for bowing, stepping and twirling slowly with a partner.
minuet-in-g.story: Christian Petzold, an organist in Dresden, wrote this minuet as part of a harpsichord suite. It was copied into the music notebook Johann Sebastian Bach gave his wife Anna Magdalena in 1725, so for about 250 years everyone thought Bach wrote it. Research by Hans-Joachim Schulze, published around 1980, identified Petzold.
minuet-in-g.funFact: In 1965 the pop group The Toys turned it into a hit song called 'A Lover's Concerto', which reached number two in America.
minuet-in-g.myth: Widely called 'Bach's Minuet in G'. It is by Christian Petzold; Bach's notebook simply contained a copy.

polly-wolly-doodle.aboutKids: A silly, happy singalong full of funny nonsense words, sung all day long on a trip to visit a friend.
polly-wolly-doodle.story: No one knows who wrote it. It probably began on the 19th-century American minstrel stage as a 'walk-around', a finale where each performer sang a verse, and was popular around the 1860s. The first known printing is in Students' Songs, a Harvard songbook from 1880. It later became a children's singalong.
polly-wolly-doodle.funFact: Its tune was borrowed for the 1979 Boney M. pop hit 'Hooray! Hooray! It's a Holi-Holiday'.
polly-wolly-doodle.myth: Often credited to minstrel songwriter Dan Emmett, but there is no real evidence that he wrote it.

rondo-alla-turca.aboutKids: A bouncy, marching tune that sounds like a parade band coming down the street with booming drums and jingly bells.
rondo-alla-turca.story: Mozart wrote this as the last movement of his Piano Sonata in A major, K. 331, around 1783, and it was published in Vienna in 1784. Viennese audiences loved anything Turkish, and the music imitates the drums and cymbals of Ottoman Janissary military bands. It is now one of Mozart's best-known tunes.
rondo-alla-turca.funFact: Some pianos around 1800 had a special Janissary pedal that rang a bell and thumped like a drum, and pianists used it in this piece.

silent-night.writtenBy: Words: Joseph Mohr. Music: Franz Xaver Gruber. English words: John Freeman Young
silent-night.aboutKids: A soft, sleepy Christmas lullaby about a calm, quiet, starry night when a tiny baby is born.
silent-night.story: Joseph Mohr, a young priest, wrote the words in 1816. In 1818 he asked schoolteacher Franz Xaver Gruber for a tune with guitar accompaniment, and they first sang it on Christmas Eve at St Nicholas Church in Oberndorf. Travelling folk singers spread it across Europe, and John Freeman Young's 1859 English version is the one most sung today.
silent-night.funFact: Silent Night has been translated into about 300 languages, and Austria lists it as part of its cultural heritage with UNESCO.
silent-night.myth: Often said mice chewed the church organ, so the song was written for guitar. There is no evidence of mice; the organ may have been damaged by flooding, and the broken-organ story was popularized by a fictional 1930s American tale.

the-blue-danube-waltz.aboutKids: A swirly, twirly waltz that sounds like a big river flowing along while dancers spin round and round.
the-blue-danube-waltz.story: Johann Strauss II, Vienna's 'Waltz King', wrote it in 1866 as a piece for a men's choir, first sung in Vienna in February 1867. He then turned it into an orchestral piece for the 1867 Paris World's Fair, where it became a sensation. It is now a beloved symbol of Austria, played at Vienna's New Year's concerts.
the-blue-danube-waltz.funFact: Composer Johannes Brahms once signed a fan with its opening notes and wrote 'Unfortunately not by Johannes Brahms'.
the-blue-danube-waltz.myth: Often said the first performance was a flop. Vienna newspapers at the time called it a hit, though the choral premiere was a more modest success than the orchestral version later in Paris.

toreador-march.aboutKids: A proud, bold march for a brave hero who strides in while the whole crowd cheers, claps and waves.
toreador-march.story: Georges Bizet wrote it for his opera Carmen, set in Spain, which opened in Paris on 3 March 1875. It is the entrance song of Escamillo, a famous bullfighter. Early audiences were unsure about the opera, and Bizet died that June, before it became a worldwide success. Carmen is now among the most performed operas.
toreador-march.funFact: Bizet never visited Spain, even though Carmen is set there and is full of Spanish-style dances.

turkey-in-the-straw.aboutKids: A fast, toe-tapping fiddle tune for stomping, clapping and square dancing in a big wooden barn.
turkey-in-the-straw.story: The tune was first printed around 1834 as 'Zip Coon', a minstrel-show song whose original lyrics mocked Black Americans. In 1861 performer Dan Bryant published 'Turkey in de Straw', ending with this melody, and the new name stuck. It became a favorite of fiddlers and square dances, usually played without words.
turkey-in-the-straw.funFact: Mickey Mouse plays this tune in Steamboat Willie (1928), one of the first cartoons with sound matched to the pictures.

yankee-doodle.origin: British North America (now the United States)
yankee-doodle.aboutKids: A silly marching song about a man who rides his pony into town and sticks a feather in his hat to look fancy.
yankee-doodle.story: The tune is older than the words. British soldiers sang early verses during the wars of the 1750s and 1760s to tease colonial American troops as country bumpkins. During the American Revolution, Americans adopted the song with their own verses and sang it proudly, and it has been an American favorite ever since.
yankee-doodle.funFact: In the 1770s, 'macaroni' did not mean pasta. It was slang for a flashy, very fashionable young man.
yankee-doodle.myth: Often said British army surgeon Richard Shuckburgh wrote it in New York around 1755. This is a popular story, but it is unproven, and the early dates are disputed.
